<blockquote>
<p><strong>Watch out:</strong> The singular values of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span></span></span></span> are <strong>not</strong> its eigenvalues. This <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span></span></span></span> is triangular with eigenvalues 3 and 5, but singular values <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.708</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.708</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">6.708</span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.236</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.236</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">2.236</span></span></span></span>. For a symmetric matrix the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues (more generally this holds for <em>normal</em> matrices, those with <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^TA = AA^T</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8413em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8413em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>), and for a positive semidefinite matrix they are exactly the eigenvalues.</p>
</blockquote>
<h2 id="Geometry-rotate-stretch-rotate"><a href="#Geometry-rotate-stretch-rotate" class="headerlink" title="Geometry: rotate, stretch, rotate"></a>Geometry: rotate, stretch, rotate</h2>
<p>Read <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A = U\Sigma V^T</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8413em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em;">U</span><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em;">V</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> from right to left as three steps applied to the unit circle:</p>
<ol>
<li><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^T</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8413em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em;">V</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is orthogonal: it rotates (or reflects) the plane, carrying <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_1, v_2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.03588em;">v</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t <p><img src="/blog/assets/linalg/diagram_05_svd_geometry.svg" alt="The SVD of A = [[3,0],[4,5]] as three steps applied to the unit circle: V transpose rotates by -45 degrees taking v1 and v2 to e1 and e2, Sigma stretches by 3 root 5 and root 5 into an axis-aligned ellipse, and U rotates by about 71.6 degrees; the result is the image of the unit circle under A, an ellipse with semi-axes along u1 and u2."></p>
<p>So <strong>every</strong> linear map of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^n</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span mathnormal mtight">n</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> sends the unit sphere to an ellipsoid (flattened when <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span></span></span></span> is singular); the singular values are its semi-axes, the <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_i</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.5806em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">u</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> their directions, and the <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_i</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.5806em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" In general <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em;">U</span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em;">V</span></span></span></span> may include a reflection; both can be chosen as rotations exactly when <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>det</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\det A \ge 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8304em;vertical-align:-0.136em;"></span><span class="mop">det</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">≥</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span> (for square <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span></span></span></span>).</p>

<h2 id="Low-rank-approximation"><a href="#Low-rank-approximation" class="headerlink" title="Low-rank approximation"></a>Low-rank approximation</h2>

For a <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1000</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k = 50</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">50</span></span></span></span>, that is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math Whether the result looks acceptable depends on how fast the singular values decay.</p>
<h2 id="The-pseudoinverse"><a href="#The-pseudoinverse" class="headerlink" title="The pseudoinverse"></a>The pseudoinverse</h2>
<p>The <strong>Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse</strong> of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A = U\Sigma V^T</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8413em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em;">U</span><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.22222em;">V</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is</p>

<p>where <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation <p><strong>Example.</strong> <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true">(</mo><mtable <h2 id="Principal-component-analysis"><a href="#Principal-component-analysis" class="headerlink" title="Principal component analysis"></a>Principal component analysis</h2>
<p>Put <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span> data points in <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^p</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6889em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.6644em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">p</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> as the rows of a matrix and subtract the mean of each column, giving a centred <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N \times p</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7667em;vertical-align:-0.0833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em;"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span> matrix <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07847em;">X</span></span></span></span>. The <strong>sample covariance matrix</strong> is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation The first component explains <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>36</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">%</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">36/(36 + 4) = 90\%</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">36/</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">36</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em;"></span><span class="mbin">+</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">4</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8056em;vertical-align:-0.0556em;"></span><span class="mord">90%</span></span></span></span> of the total variance.</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Common pitfall:</strong> Forgetting to centre the data. Without subtracting the mean, the first &quot;principal component&quot; mostly points at the mean itself. Also scale the columns first when they are in different units, or the largest-unit variable dominates.</p>
</blockquote>

<p><strong>6.</strong> Prove that if <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8778em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span></span></span></span> is orthogonal then every real eigenvalue of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8778em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span></span></span></span> is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7278em;vertical-align:-0.0833em;"></span><span class="mord">±</span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span>, and every singular value of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8778em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span></span></span></span> is 1.</p>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>
<p>If <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8889em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.03588em;">v</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel"><span class="mrel"><span class="mord vbox"><span class="thinbox"><span class="rlap"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8889em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="inner"><span class="mord"><span class="mrel"></span></span></span><span style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span>, then <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">∥</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">∥</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">∥</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>v</mi><mo class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em;"></span><span class="mopen">∥</span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.03588em;">v</span><span class="mclose">∥</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" Singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q^TQ = I</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1.0358em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8413em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.07847em;">I</span></span></span></span>, all equal to 1: an orthogonal map sends the unit sphere to itself.</p>
</details>
<p><strong>7.</strong> Show that for a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix the SVD and the spectral decomposition coincide, and give a <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2 \times 2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.7278em;vertical-align:-0.0833em;"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em;"></span><span class="mbin">×</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> symmetric matrix where they differ.</p>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>
<p>If <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8444em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span <h1 id="Whats-next"><a href="#Whats-next" class="headerlink" title="What's next"></a>What's next</h1>
<p>This completes the base series: from solving <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Ax = b</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">A</span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">b</span></span></span></span> by elimination (post 00) to the SVD, which describes any matrix completely by two orthonormal bases and a list of stretch factors. The table below lists the posts planned to extend the series. The most natural next step is canonical forms — the full proof of the Jordan form stated in Linear Algebra 04 — followed by the numerical side, where the algorithms behind <code>numpy.linalg</code> (LU with pivoting, Householder QR, the QR eigenvalue algorithm, Golub–Kahan SVD) are studied for speed and accuracy.</p>

<h1 id="References"><a href="#References" class="headerlink" title="References"></a>References</h1>
<ul>
<li>Sheldon Axler, <em>Linear Algebra Done Right</em>, 4th ed., Springer (2024) — Chapter 6 (inner product spaces, Gram–Schmidt, orthogonal projection, least squares) and Chapter 7 (self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem, positive operators, SVD). Open access at <a href="https://linear.axler.net/" target="_blank" rel="noopener external nofollow noreferrer">linear.axler.net</a>.</li>
<li>Gilbert Strang, <em>Introduction to Linear Algebra</em>, 6th ed., Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2023) — orthogonality, projections, least squares, Gram–Schmidt; symmetric and positive definite matrices; the SVD and PCA.</li>
<li>Gilbert Strang, <em>Linear Algebra and Learning from Data</em>, Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2019) — the SVD, Eckart–Young, PCA and low-rank approximation from the data-science side.</li>
<li>Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, <em>Numerical Linear Algebra</em>, SIAM (1997) — Lectures 4–5 (SVD), 6–11 (projectors, QR, Gram–Schmidt, Householder, least squares), 12–15 (conditioning and stability).</li>
<li>Gene H. Golub, Charles F. Van Loan, <em>Matrix Computations</em>, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins University Press (2013) — the reference for QR, SVD and least-squares algorithms.</li>
<li>Roger A. Horn, Charles R. Johnson, <em>Matrix Analysis</em>, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2012) — positive definite matrices, the spectral theorem and the SVD with complete proofs.</li>
<li>Carl Eckart, Gale Young, &quot;The approximation of one matrix by another of lower rank&quot;, <em>Psychometrika</em> 1 (1936), 211–218 — the original low-rank approximation theorem.</li>
<li>MIT OpenCourseWare, <a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06-linear-algebra-spring-2010/" target="_blank" rel="noopener external nofollow noreferrer">18.06 Linear Algebra (Spring 2010), Gilbert Strang</a> — lectures 14–17 (orthogonality, projections, least squares, Gram–Schmidt), 25 and 27 (symmetric and positive definite matrices) and 29 (SVD); and <a href="https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-065-matrix-methods-in-data-analysis-signal-processing-and-machine-learning-spring-2018/" target="_blank" rel="noopener external nofollow noreferrer">18.065 Matrix Methods in Data Analysis, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning (Spring 2018)</a>.</li>
